title: Judges 8:18–21
context: Judges 8:18–21 reveals a personal dimension to Gideon’s pursuit of Zebah and Zalmunna. Questioned about the men they killed at Tabor, the kings say they resembled Gideon, and Gideon declares they were his brothers, the sons of his mother. He swears that he would have spared the kings if they had spared his brothers, then orders his young son Jether to kill them. When the boy hesitates, Gideon kills the kings himself and takes the crescent ornaments from their camels. The earlier killing at Tabor is not narrated elsewhere in Judges, and the scene reads as an act of personal and family vengeance as well as the execution of enemy kings.

verses.text: Then he said to Zebah and Zalmunna, “What kind of men were they whom you killed at Tabor?” They answered, “They were like you. They all resembled the children of a king.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon asks the kings about “men … whom you killed at Tabor,” and they answer, “They were like you. They all resembled the children of a king.” Arminian readers note that this reveals a personal motive for the pursuit that the narrative had not yet disclosed, adding a human dimension to Gideon’s actions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the kings’ reply may be meant as flattery or defiance, and the phrase “children of a king” quietly anticipates the question of kingship in 8:22–23. Shared ground: both traditions read the exchange as showing that Gideon’s campaign has become personal, and both read the scene within the narrative’s developing portrait of Gideon.

verses.text: He said, “They were my brothers, the sons of my mother. As the LORD lives, if you had saved them alive, I would not kill you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon says, “They were my brothers, the sons of my mother,” and swears, “As the LORD lives, if you had saved them alive, I would not kill you.” Arminian readers note that Gideon frames the execution as just retribution for the killing of his brothers, invoking the LORD’s name in an oath.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the oath uses the LORD’s name, yet the motive expressed is family vengeance rather than a divine command. The narrator lets the reader weigh the difference. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing a mixture of justice and personal motive, and both caution against reading Gideon’s words as a straightforward model.

verses.text: He said to Jether his firstborn, “Get up and kill them!” But the youth didn’t draw his sword; for he was afraid, because he was yet a youth.
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon tells his firstborn Jether to kill the kings, but the youth is afraid. Arminian readers note the human detail: the boy’s fear echoes Gideon’s own early fear (6:15; 7:10). Gideon seems to want to give his son the honor of the act, but the boy is unwilling.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the episode underscores the shift in Gideon’s concerns toward family honor and his own house, themes that come to the fore in 8:22–35. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a poignant moment, and both note how it prepares for the questions of dynasty raised in the following verses.

verses.text: Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, “You rise and fall on us; for as the man is, so is his strength.” Gideon arose, and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, and took the crescents that were on their camels’ necks.
verses.arminianNotes: The kings challenge Gideon, “You rise and fall on us; for as the man is, so is his strength,” and he kills them and takes the crescents from their camels. Arminian readers note that the kings face death with defiance, and that Gideon’s taking of the ornaments foreshadows the gold of 8:24–26.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the crescents, royal ornaments, will reappear among the gold used for the ephod (8:26). The detail quietly links the victory to the snare that follows. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as completing the judgment on Midian’s kings and as a narrative hinge leading into the closing scenes of Gideon’s life.
